Specific information for this practical exam
During the exam, the supervisor or other competent biologist (not the invigilator) should obtain the
results needed for the supervisor’s report by following the relevant steps in the question paper. The
results should be recorded in the supervisor’s report.
Organisation of the exam
Ɣ
All candidates must have access to the materials required for Question 1 throughout the whole
period of the exam.
Ɣ
Half of the candidates will have access to the microscope and slide for a maximum time of one
hour from the start of the exam. These candidates should start with Question 2. After one hour, or
sooner if candidates have finished Question 2, they should move on to Question 1.
Ɣ
For Question 2, two candidates are not permitted to share the same microscope and slide at the
same time.
Ɣ
The other candidates should start with Question 1. After one hour, these candidates should be
given access to the microscope and slide. They should then move on to Question 2 as soon as
they are ready.
Ɣ
Candidates will only have access to the microscope and slide for one hour. They should be
advised that they can answer any part of the exam paper not requiring the microscope and slide
throughout the whole period of the exam.
Ɣ
Access arrangements to microscopes and slides, including instructions on which question to start
with and timings, must be explained to candidates before the start of the exam.
Materials to be supplied by Cambridge International
Ɣ
Slide P1
On receipt of the slides, check that they are labelled P1 and that no slides are broken. The slides
should not be viewed in advance of the exam. The material on the slides is confidential and must
not be disclosed to candidates.
The number of slides supplied by Cambridge International will be equal to half the candidate entry.
Return of slides to Cambridge International
Immediately after the exam, the slides must be:
Ɣ

self-adhesive label supplied. The slides must not be included in the packet of scripts.
or

purchased using the order form enclosed with the slides, which should be completed and returned
to Cambridge International. The order form must not be included in the packet of scripts. Slides

If the slides are not returned or purchased by the deadline stated on the order form, the charge will be
£3.75 per slide plus £1 per box.

distilled water. Mix well.

R1, S and the stock solution of iodine (0.1 mol dm–3) may be prepared the day before the exam.
Each solution should be kept in a covered container in a refrigerator overnight.
The 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution must be prepared no more than one hour before the start of the
exam.
R1 and S should be at room temperature before the start of the exam.
Ɣ
R1 and S, 1.0% starch suspension
These are prepared by putting 1 g of soluble starch into a small volume of distilled water and
mixing to make a paste. Make up to 100 cm3 with hot distilled water. Heat the suspension to
dissolve the starch, mixing well.
These starch suspensions must be at room temperature for the exam.
Ɣ
iodine, 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine in potassium iodide solution
This is prepared by making a 0.1 mol dm–3 stock solution of iodine, then diluting it to make the
0.01 mol dm–3 solution:
–
Put 8.0 g of potassium iodide in a beaker or container.
–
Add 2 cm3 of distilled water to moisten the potassium iodide.
–
Add 2.5 g of iodine [MH][N] (if necessary, crush to small pieces) to the moist potassium
iodide.
–
Add 15 cm3 of distilled water and stir well.
–
When no more iodine dissolves, add another 15 cm3 of distilled water and stir well.
–
Repeat with two more volumes of 15 cm3 of distilled water and then make up to a total volume
of 100 cm3. It is not essential that all the iodine dissolves.
This gives a red-brown coloured 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution.
–
Put 10 cm3 of the 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution into a beaker or container.
–
Make up to 100 cm3 with distilled water. Mix well.
This makes the 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution and is a yellow-orange colour.
Prepare the 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution no more than one hour before the exam.

Preparation of materials
The beetroot should be prepared the day before the exam and kept in a covered container in a
refrigerator.
All the materials should be at room temperature before the start of the exam.
Ɣ
B, pieces of beetroot, in water, in a beaker or container with a suitable cover to prevent evaporation.
The plant tissue you may use is any purple variety of beetroot, Beta vulgaris.
The beetroot should be uncooked and as fresh as possible to avoid the effects of storage.
Four cylinders of beetroot are needed per candidate.
To prepare the beetroot:

use a cork borer with a diameter of 8–10 mm to cut cylinders of beetroot 30–40 mm long
–
remove the outer skin at each end of the cylinders
–
put the prepared beetroot cylinders into a beaker or container and cover with water
–
change the water several times to remove as much of the pigment as possible
–
leave the beetroot cylinders soaking in the water overnight
–
before the exam, change the water several times
–
for each candidate put 4 of the cylinders into a small beaker covered with distilled water.

The responses of plant species to water stress can be classified as either isohydric or anisohydric.
•
Isohydric plant species close stomata during times of water stress. This behaviour minimises
water loss by transpiration but also reduces carbon dioxide uptake for photosynthesis.
•
Anisohydric plant species do not close stomata during times of water stress. This behaviour
maximises carbon dioxide uptake for photosynthesis but also increases water loss
by transpiration.

Tumours may be described as benign or malignant. Malignant tumours can lead to greater
complications for the person with the tumour.
Early identification of tumours, particularly malignant tumours, is important for effective treatment.
Benign tumour cells and malignant tumour cells can look similar when viewed using a light
microscope.
Some scientists wanted to develop a diagnostic test to identify tumour cells as benign or malignant.
The scientists investigated whether the diameter of the cell nucleus could be used to identify the
type of tumour cell as benign or malignant.
The scientists used a light microscope with a calibrated eyepiece graticule to measure the
diameter of the nuclei of stained tumour cells.

Preparation of materials
SM and CM should be prepared on the day of the exam.
Each solution should be kept in a covered container until required. Solutions should be at room
temperature before the start of the exam.
The iodine solution can be prepared the day before the exam and stored in the dark until required.
Ɣ
SM, 1.0% starch solution in milk
Add 1 g of soluble starch to 5 cm3 of warmed milk to make a paste. Stir the paste into 80 cm3 of
warmed milk and make up to 100 cm3 using more milk. Heat the milk to almost boiling (at least
75–80 'C), stirring constantly to fully dissolve the starch.
Ɣ
CM, 0.02% starch solution in milk
This is prepared by diluting 2 cm3 of the 1.0% starch solution, SM, with 98 cm3 of milk. Mix well.
Ɣ
iodine, 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution
To prepare a 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution:
–
put 8.0 g of potassium iodide in a beaker or container
–
add 2 cm3 of distilled water to moisten the potassium iodide
–
add 2.5 g of iodine [MH][N] (if necessary, crush to small pieces) to the moist potassium iodide
–
add 15 cm3 of distilled water and stir well
–
when no more iodine dissolves, add another 15 cm3 of distilled water and stir well
–
repeat with two more volumes of 15 cm3 of distilled water
–
make up to a total volume of 100 cm3
–
put 10 cm3 of this 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution into a beaker or container
–
make up to 100 cm3 with distilled water
–
mix well.

Iodine solution (0.1 mol dm–3) should be prepared the day before the exam and kept in a
covered container in a refrigerator. 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution needs to be diluted to make the
0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution no more than one hour before the start of the exam. This needs to be
at room temperature before the start of the exam.
S1, S2, S3 and U can be prepared the day before the exam. They should be kept in covered
containers in a refrigerator. Solutions should be at room temperature before the start of the exam.
Ɣ
iodine, 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine solution
Prepare a 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution the day before the exam:
–
put 8.0 g of potassium iodide in a beaker
–
add 2 cm3 of distilled water to moisten the potassium iodide
–
add 2.5 g of iodine [MH][N] (if necessary, crush to small pieces) to the moist potassium iodide
–
add 15 cm3 of distilled water and stir well.
When no more iodine dissolves:
–
add another 15 cm3 of distilled water and stir well
–
repeat with two more volumes of 15 cm3 of distilled water
–
make up to a total volume of 100 cm3.
It is not essential that all the iodine dissolves.
This forms a red-brown coloured, 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution.
On the day of the exam, dilute the 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution to make the 0.01 mol dm–3 iodine
solution:

put 10 cm3 of 0.1 mol dm–3 iodine solution into a beaker or container
–
make up to 100 cm3 with distilled water
–
mix well.

Specific information for this practical exam
During the exam, the supervisor or other competent biologist (not the invigilator) should obtain the
results needed for the supervisor’s report by following the relevant steps in the question paper. The
results should be recorded in the supervisor’s report.
Organisation of the exam
Ɣ
All candidates must have access to the materials required for Question 1 throughout the whole
period of the exam.
Ɣ
Half of the candidates will have access to the microscope and slide for a maximum time of one
hour from the start of the exam. These candidates should start with Question 2. After one hour, or
sooner if candidates have finished Question 2, they should move on to Question 1.
Ɣ
For Question 2, two candidates are not permitted to share the same microscope and slide at the
same time.
Ɣ
The other candidates should start with Question 1. After one hour, these candidates should be
given access to the microscope and slide. They should then move on to Question 2 as soon as
they are ready.
Ɣ
Candidates will only have access to the microscope and slide for one hour. They should be
advised that they can answer any part of the exam paper not requiring the microscope and slide
throughout the whole period of the exam.
Ɣ
Access arrangements to microscopes and slides, including instructions on which question to start
with and timings, must be explained to candidates before the start of the exam.

Starch grains are present in plant cells. The starch grains have different sizes and shapes
depending on the type of plant.
As the starch grains get larger, patterns form on the surface of the starch grains. These patterns
can be observed using a microscope.
You are provided with samples from two different plants, C and D.
You will need to:
•
prepare a microscope slide of starch grains from C and D
•
observe the starch grains present on each microscope slide

draw two starch grains from each sample.

step 2

step 3

step 4
Cut this slice into smaller pieces.
step 5
Put two drops of distilled water onto these small pieces.
step 6
Use a teat pipette to transfer drops of the liquid from around the small pieces prepared in
step 5 onto the slide labelled C.
step 7
Put a coverslip over the liquid on slide C.
step 8
Use the microscope to observe the starch grains on slide C.
You may need to reduce the amount of light entering the microscope and will need to adjust the
fine focus to observe the surface of the starch grains clearly.
step 9
